requirement: In a book chapter, each valid `{impl}`, `{cite}`, or `{test}` reference, inline or fenced, MUST render as a Shields.io static badge image with meaningful alt text that displays its role and full name and links to the badge at the corresponding `{req}` or `{example}` definition. Links MUST work across chapters, including nested chapters. A fenced reference MUST render its badge followed by its body as Markdown. Each fenced `{req}` or `{example}` directive MUST render as a Shields.io definition badge image identifying its kind; text outside a directive MUST remain literal. Badge text MUST remain legible regardless of whether its link has been visited. A badge link MUST show a visible indicator when it has keyboard focus and MAY brighten on hover. Badges MAY be laid out inline with the surrounding text, a fenced reference's badge and body MAY be visually set apart from the surrounding text as one block, and a built-in's unlinked badge MAY show a help cursor to signal its hover text. These badges use the syntax defined by {cite}`requirements.references.targets`.
rationale:
**Judgment: the requirement is met.** The code marked `{impl}` implements every obligation, and the tests cover the main cases and failure cases.

**Implementation**
- **Reference badges.** `reference_badge` and `shield_badge` (src/lib.rs) render each valid `{impl}`, `{cite}` or `{test}` reference as a Shields.io static badge image. The alt text is `"<role> <full name>"`, and the badge links to `<target path>#habeas-req-…` or `#habeas-example-…`.
  - `ReferenceKind::label` and `ReferenceKind::color` give the role and colour.
  - `DefinitionKind::anchor` gives the anchor name.
  - `replace_inline_references` handles inline references.
  - `replace_references` handles fenced ones.
- **Cross-chapter and nested links.** `chapter_href` builds relative links, including `../` from nested chapters, and encodes `.md` so mdBook leaves the URL alone.
- **Fenced references.** `replace_references` uses `fenced::markdown_fences` to find fences. `markdown_fences` and `MarkdownFence` (src/fenced.rs) leave fences in code or raw HTML literal. Each closed fence becomes a `<div class="habeas-fenced-ref">` holding the badge, then the body rendered recursively as Markdown.
- **Definition badges.** `replace_definitions` renders each fenced `{req}` or `{example}` directive as a Shields.io badge. `DefinitionKind::badge` supplies the `req` or `example` label, and the badge links to a detail page when one exists. Invalid names, unclosed fences and text outside directives stay literal.
- **Stylesheet.** `md/habeas.css` is anchored with `:impl:` in the requirement declaration. It does the following:
  - Visited badge links inherit their colour, so they look the same as unvisited ones.
  - Badge links get a visible `outline` on `:focus-visible`.
  - Badge links brighten on `:hover`.
  - Badges are laid out inline.
  - Built-in badges get `cursor: help`.
  - Fenced references are visually set apart as a block.
  - All of these are options or obligations the requirement permits, and the stylesheet's selectors are limited to Habeas badge classes.
- **Marking.** Every part of the implementation carries an `{impl}`. Behaviour beyond this requirement, such as the "See evidence" link and detail-page links, is marked with the requirements that specify it (`requirements.index.navigation`, `requirements.references.safe_badges`, `requirements.references.builtin_definitions` and others).

**Tests**
- `fenced_references_render_their_badge_and_body_and_built_ins_are_unlinked` covers these cases:
  - The fenced badge precedes its body, and the body is rendered as Markdown.
  - The fenced badge links to the definition.
  - A built-in badge is unlinked and its hover text is the built-in's text.
  - An inline reference to a built-in, an unknown name, and a reference inside a code fence all stay literal.
- `references_in_nested_chapters_link_to_the_requirement_definition` checks `impl`, `cite` and `test` badges from `guides/deep.md`. It asserts the `../requirements.html#habeas-req-…` link and the Shields URL with the right role and colour.
- `examples_are_distinct_definitions_and_tests_link_to_them` checks the example definition badge (`alt="example …"`), links to examples, and that invalid or code-fenced directives stay literal.
- `colon_directives_render_markdown_bodies_and_legacy_roles_stay_literal` checks Markdown bodies and that text outside directives stays literal.
- `shields_badge_urls_escape_requirement_names` checks the badge URL and alt text, including the `req` label.
- `badge_stylesheet_keeps_visited_links_legible_and_shows_focus` checks that visited links match unvisited ones, the focus outline, the hover brightness, and that only Habeas selectors are styled. It uses the helper `stylesheet_rules`.

The tests do not assert the `cursor: help` rule or the fenced block border. The requirement only permits both (MAY), and the selector-whitelist check covers their rules.

No acknowledged FIXMEs or gaps remain.

Project text files MAY use the `{impl}`, `{cite}`, and `{test}` roles with a backtick-delimited full requirement or example name, or with a built-in name under {cite}`requirements.references.builtin_definitions`. A reference MAY instead be written in fenced form, `:::{role} name` on one line, a body, and a closing fence, following the fence rules of {cite}`requirements.ci.span` and {cite}`requirements.ci.fence_lengths`; the fenced form is the same edge with attached commentary, and the inline form carries none. In a source comment, fence lines MUST be recognized after removing each line's comment delimiters within one comment run under {cite}`requirements.references.outline_comments`, and a fence that does not close within its comment run MUST be a validation error. Each reference is a directed edge between its source and the named definition. A source is a project source item or a requirement or example declaration. `{cite}` MUST mean that the source relies on, supports, or refers to the definition, and is an edge from the source to the definition. `{impl}` MUST mean that the source implements part of the definition: it makes a decision, performs a check, produces an output, or handles a case that the definition specifies. A requirement MAY implement part of another requirement by refining one of its obligations. Calling code that implements a definition, or producing a result a caller uses to meet it, MUST NOT by itself count as implementing it. A requirement stating a convention for every output of a kind, such as every validation error, is implemented by the source that carries out the convention as a whole, such as the step that collects and reports those outputs. `{test}` MUST mean that the source is designed to verify behavior the definition specifies: a test through its scenario and the assertions about that scenario's outcome, or a named example through the concrete case it describes. `{impl}` and `{test}` are edges from the definition to the source. Only requirements and examples are assessed; code is reviewed as part of the definitions it implements or tests. Habeas MUST find these references throughout project source files and MUST fail with the source file and line if a name has no matching `{req}` or `{example}` definition. In Markdown, escaped roles and roles in code examples MUST remain literal. Reference discovery MUST consider exactly the project sources that source-access policy permits under {cite}`requirements.authoring.source_tools`: in a Git worktree, files present in the Git index, including staged new files; outside Git, all project files; in both cases excluding the project-root `book` and `evidence` directories, `.git` and `target` directories at any depth, and paths disallowed by {cite}`requirements.configuration.evidence_paths`. Evidence snapshots and generated build output MUST therefore not be counted as source references.
